articles.text: The city commissioned a herd of 500 goats through Ecosystem Concepts in Dixon, a company that pioneered the use of goats to take out undergrowth that fuels the flames of wildfires. The company emerged after the 1991 wildfire in Oakland in order to “provide a sustainable solution.” The goats came to Piedmont on June 20 and will return to a quieter area away from the sound of fireworks tomorrow, July 2. The herd will be moved before Independence Day weekend because the sound of fireworks can make the goats anxious, Fire Chief Bret Black explained. Goatherd Martin Matarrese answered questions from residents on Tuesday afternoon at a public event created by Chief Black. The herd can clear unwanted, dry brush in areas and steep hills where machinery or chemicals cannot. Each goat will eat approximately 10 pounds of brush or grass a day, Matarrese said. The goats cleared approximately 50 percent of the undergrowth in Blair Park in two days. The goats stay in one place until they collectively eat about four to six inches of vegetation and grass. Staff Photos A group of 500 goats were brought to Piedmont for the past week to help clear brush and weeds on the hillside above Coaches Field and in Blair Park. The herd of 500 that arrived in Piedmont is young, with an average age of one year, Matarrese said. “The sites [in Piedmont] are mostly steep, and the soil is soft. These are lighter-weight goats, as opposed to the up to six-yearold goats in some of our bigger herds,” he said. Their life expectancy is about seven to eight years. At that age, the goat’s teeth begin to soften, and they can no longer graze. Two dogs stayed on-site with the herd to protect them from natural predators, such as mountain lions or coyotes. Matarrese said that coyote sightings have recently become more prevalent in the Bay Area, so the dogs stay with the goats throughout the night to ensure their safety. Border Collies are used as “sheep herders,” and assist the goatherd in transporting the goats from one location to the next. Ecosystem Concepts has a total of about 5000 goats, and has contracts with a number of cities, including Oakland, Roseville, and Menlo Park. They are also used by homeowners associations across northern California.
articles.title: Goats come calling in Piedmont

articles.text: Oakland firefighters blamed fireworks for an early morning brushfire in the Oakland hills on Sunday, June 28, days after the Piedmont Fire Department warned that the use of any fireworks, including sparklers, can cause wildfires. Reported in the middle of the night, at 3:09 a.m. on Sunday, the three-alarm fire burned about 2.5 acres near the intersection of Crest Avenue and Fontaine Street by Interstate 580. No structures were threatened by the fire and no one was injured, but Oakland Fire Department confirmed that it took 56 firefighters several hours to extinguish the intense fire. Oakland firefighters said that the cause was the use of illegal fireworks. articles.text: Editor: Last week the City of Piedmont sent the following message to all residents. “We owe it to each other to wear a face covering! We are all working towards the common goal of not spreading the Covid-19 virus, and as cases have increased across the nation, we must do all we can to prevent increased numbers in Piedmont. Alameda County’s updated face covering order issued on June 5th mandates that face coverings be worn at all times in public if you are or are likely to be within 30 feet of another person outside of your household. 30 feet is roughly the length of 2 cars. There is NO EXEMPTION for persons engaged in exercise. The face covering does not have to be worn the whole time exercising, but it must be carried and then put on when within 30 feet of other people.” I am saddened to see more than a few Piedmonters who are not adhering to these mandates. Many are 20 and younger but there is a lot of representation from those 30 and older, including more than a few who are over 60. I am close to being an octogenarian and have over 50 years of experience as a physician, educator and research scientist. I am an Emeritus Professor of Medicine and Gastroenterology at UCSF and an Emeritus Investigator at Kaiser Northern CA Division of Research. I have many friends and colleagues who are epidemiologists and one who is an Emeritus Infectious Disease expert at UCB and who is quoted often in the media on issues pertaining to COVID19. When I query maskless runners and walkers about why they are not masked, the following are their answers: 1. The mask isn’t necessary because I am outside 2. The mask isn’t necessary because I am not a Senior Citizen 3. The mask isn’t necessary because I am at a 6-foot distance from you My questions for your readers are: --What can we as concerned citizens do to encourage compliance in our community - i.e. educational town hall gatherings, Zoom conferences, etc. --Is there enforcement of these mandates in Piedmont? Who is responsible for it? I have witnessed none. As the virus surges, younger people account for “disturbing” number of cases People in their 20s, 30s and 40s account for a growing proportion of the cases in many places, raising fears that asymptomatic young people are helping to fuel the virus’s spread. See the following article in the New York Times: https://www.nytimes. com/2020/06/25/us/coronavirus-cases-young-people.html -James Allison, MD

articles.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a budget emergency in order to release funds to help pay for resources needed to combat the COVID-19 pandemic. Citing a $54.3 billion state budget deficit, Newsom declared the emergency on Thursday morning, June 25. The proclamation states that the ongoing pandemic “requires future expenditures of state funds for personal protective equipment (PPE), medical equipment and other expenditures as necessary to support a potential hospital surge, to provide necessary services to vulnerable populations, and other expenditures necessary to respond to the threat and spread of COVID-19.” The proclamation specifies that the state must use a portion of the reserves in the Budget Stabilization Account in the 2020-21 fiscal year to fund expenditures related to COVID-19 and provide other needed services. California has experienced a sharp increase in hospitalizations for more than a week and last week set daily records for new cases since the mandate to lockdown in March. The state broke a record on Tuesday, June 23 with an increase of more than 7000 cases in 24 hours. Newsom suggested that the rise in cases is due to Californians’ cavalier attitude toward the virus. “Many of us understandably developed a little cabin fever. Some of us, I would argue, developed a little amnesia. Others have frankly taken down their guard,” the governor said during a June 24 press briefing. “People are mixing and that is increasing the spread of the virus,” he added.
articles.title: Gov. Newsom declares budget emergency to fund COVID-19 response

articles.text: All three banks in Piedmont – Wells Fargo, Citi Bank, and Bank of America – have remained closed to customers throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. The three banks officially closed on March 16, without warning to customers. Banks and related financial institutions, including money lender and check cashing services, are considered essential businesses and are permitted to remain open throughout the health crisis. However, the decision to remain open is ultimately up to each bank and its district manager. Some brick-and-mortar banks closed their doors to customers in anticipation of lower foot traffic. Wells Fargo District Manager Munir Ahmad said that the decision to close the location at 344 Highland Avenue was due to a shortage of employees. “We closed about 35 percent of our branches, including Piedmont, Rockridge and Claremont. Most of our team members [at the Piedmont location] chose to self-quarantine due to high risk of exposure,” Ahmad said. When asked why customers were not notified of the closure, Ahmad said that developments related to countywide restrictions were happening very quickly, making it difficult to alert customers in a timely manner. In the event of a second closure, customers will be notified by mail, according to Ahmad. Wells Fargo has said that its Piedmont branch would reopen on Monday, June 29, but the doors remained locked throughout the day. Markers have been placed outside the entrance to designate social distances of six feet, but with the bank closed, there is no evidence of customers waiting to get inside. articles.text: Editor: Last night, (Monday, June 29) the Piedmont City Council held a special online meeting on the short and long term prospects for the Piedmont Community Pool, given the age of the pool, maintenance issues resulting from the age, and the current COVID crisis. The meeting was well attended (virtually) and Piedmonters of all ages spoke overwhelmingly in favor of keeping the pool open, and working toward the replacement facility envisioned in the Aquatics Master Plan in 2016. I encourage the City Council to continue the strategy developed in 2016-17 to seek a bond measure to support city facilities as a bundled package, with the pool as one of the projects in the package. I believe that the strategy discussed last night to seek a bond for the pool by itself, competing with other bond measures on the ballot, would likely not be successful and would result in the permanent loss of a pool for Piedmont. This would be a sad loss for the many Piedmonters who enjoy the pool, and use it for recreation, exercise, and for all of the multitude of programs for young people that it has always supported. I urge the Council to stick with the prior strategy of bundling improvements in one measure. -Duncan Watry

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council will consider the first reading of an ordinance implementing Reach Codes, or amendments to the state’s Building Energy Efficiency Standards and state Electrical Code, which are designed to promote efficient building methods in homes in Piedmont. The first reading will be conducted during a regular city council meeting on July 6 at 7:30 p.m. The council will also consider an ordinance requiring home energy audits under certain circumstances. These measures are being proposed because Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 calls for the community to reduce its annual greenhouse gas emissions from the building, transportation, waste, and wastewater sectors. The goal is to reduce emissions from about 38,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions in 2017, to just 9,800 metric tons in 2050. Currently, a large percentage of the city’s emissions come from natural gas appliances in buildings, especially gas furnaces and water heaters. To meet CAP goals, the community must decrease natural gas use in buildings by improving insulation, and by switching out natural gas appliances for electric appliances powered by renewable energy. The proposed requirements are as follows: newly constructed low-rise residential buildings, including new detached accessory dwelling units (ADUs), must use all electric building appliances. Projects proposing an entire new upper level on a low-rise residential building, or that increase a low-rise residential building’s total roof area by 30 percent or more, are required to install solar panels on their roof. Additionally, a housing renovation on a low-rise residential building, that costs $25,000 or more, will require the applicant to include one item from a list of energy efficient insulation or electrification fixes. The council will also consider other amendments to the building code and policy changes that will help reduce natural gas use. Residents are encouraged to participate by submitting comments and by attending the council meeting, which will be held virtually through Zoom technology. Comments regarding the proposed code amendments may be sent to the council via email at citycouncil@piedmont.ca.gov.

Located next to Piedmont Grocery it reopened Friday, June 17 after an uneasy three months in which they employed new business strategies. Dress Best for Less (DBFL) is a non-profit thrift store stocked with donations from Piedmont’s carriage house donation center across the street from the high school. In addition to providing some funding for Piedmont schools, it contributes to charitable organizations. About one month into the county’s required shutdown due to the coronavirus, members of the DBFL board realized the restrictions were not ending anytime soon, so they created a website. Thrift stores rely on in-person browsing, so sales were low through the site. Board member Melanie Marcus saw a silver lining. “We kept our name out there and kept active. We showcased the nice labels and brands and the quality of the merchandise,” she said. Cheryl Wozniak, Director of Curriculum, presented the renewed board policy at a June 24 meeting, which was up for review as a first reading. “For many years, members of our community and PUSD staff have really had a strong interest and goal of bringing diversity work to Piedmont,” Wozniak said. A Diversity Task Force was formed in 2011, comprised of district staff and community members to create a mission and vision development. The task force formed a partnership with Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC), a community-based committee with a mission to promote and practice inclusiveness in Piedmont and surrounding communities. In 2011, the task force came before the school board to present their development mission statement, which was later incorporated into the District’s mission and goals. Wozniak said that this was a starting point for the district’s commitment to fostering inclusion and beginning to recognize structures that raise barriers, preventing all from feeling welcome and receiving an equal education experience. In 2017, the board adopted a three-year Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP). This was comprised of two goals: to ensure that all students feel physically safe, emotionally cared for, and academically as well as socially included in their school environment. The second goal was to commit to equity, diversity, and social justice partnerships and community engagement. “We can make wise decisions about what text we put in front of our students, so that they see themselves in the curriculum and have windows to the experiences of others who have different backgrounds,” Wozniak said, adding that the district has been adopting curriculum over the past few years that celebrates diversity through a social justice lens. In the past year, students have written and shared their own stories through a series entitled “I Am Here: Conservations About Identity.” Mentorship programs for Asian-American students, where high school students have partnered with elementary students, is continuing to progress. The proposal presented by Wozniak stated, “The district shall commit to anti-racist work in order to proactively identify class and cultural biases as well as practices, policies, and institutional barrier that negatively influence student learning and impede equal access to opportunities for all students.” The draft calls on the board and superintendent to develop and implement policies and strategies that promote equity by recognizing the existence of institutional racism and working to dismantle systems of oppression within district programs and activities. articles.text: Kimberly Bonacum, an Occupational Therapist, has worked in Piedmont schools for 16 years. In that time, she has worked with a wide range of students, including a number of them who fidget due to being hyperactive. To help them, she has designed and is now producing a wearable “fidget” spinner wristband that is mindful of the learning environment. It helps keep their attention during school. The product was released in March. Her company, called Mindful Fidget, has created an adaptation of the popular fidget spinner but is smaller, quieter and less likely to be misplaced because it’s attached to the wrist. “It’s great for overall calmThe Mindful Fidget has tactile bumps on its edges and a quick release to easily swap out wristbands. ing of anxiety and for overall self-regulation. It helps to get students in just the right state to learn,” explained Bonacum. She works as an OT with Piedmont students at all grade levels. OTs are sometimes asked to assist in curriculum development for handwriting and social skills, or recommend modifications to classroom environments or assignments that help all students participate. Former Havens 4th grade teacher Catherine Knowland, a Piedmont resident, sees a need for products to improve the focus of students. “The ability of students to focus has gotten worse over time. When I first started teaching in the 80s, there might have been six students in a class that needed some sort of distraction or fidget. Into the 90s with the invention of the computer and video games their attention spans got worse. Nearly all of them needed to be entertained with a hands-on item to manipulate.” The large, and loud handheld fidget spinner had an explosion of popularity in 2017. Students began to use them as toys and had competitions with each other. This became a distraction in class and eventually most schools had to ban them. Bonacum’s design is focused on being school friendly. She picked a bearing that is quiet and does not spin for too long, requiring active participation. Bonacum sees applications for patterns. adults as well. out.”

articles.text: Nick Millosovich stepped in as Piedmont’s Public Works Department Supervisor of Maintenance on April 1, six months after former Supervisor Dave Frankel retired after a 30-year career. Millosovich held the role of interim supervisor for a sixmonth period before his contract with the city was formally approved. He has worked with the city for 13 years, since 2007, the year of the city’s Centennial. Millosovich will work under the direction of Chester Nakahara, Director of the Public Works Department. “Public Works is very pleased with the appointment of Nick as our Public Works Supervisor. In his 13 years with the city, he has proven to be a caring leader with a high level of technical skills, and is a great ambassador for the department and the City of Piedmont. Going forward, I think the city is in good hands with Nick,” Nakahara said. Prior to taking on the role of Public Work Supervisor, Millosovich worked with Diamond Tree Service for approximately 16 years. Diamond Tree Service offers brush chipping, land clearing, stump removal, insect management, and cabling and bracing. Millosovich is a certified arborist with experience working in the professional tree care industry. He began working with Diamond Tree Service after the 1991 firestorm in the Oakland hills. The blaze, which raged for three days, destroyed more than 3,000 homes and burned 1,520 acres. “On my first day, I walked in wearing nice blue jeans. They told me to take this cable, wrap it around this log that was burned. When I got up, I was pitch black, covered in soot,” he said. The work that summer was taxing, but Millosovich said that he “had the best office in the world” looking over the hills. His work with Diamond Tree Service served as a catalyst for his decade-long tenure with the city, with whom Diamond Tree owner Kent Donaghy has done contract work for decades. The transition to working with the city’s Public Works Department was seamless. Piedmont’s public works department is responsible for oversight of all functions relating to infrastructure systems; this include sanitary and storm sewers, coordination of utility company systems, street maintenance and improvement, sidewalks, street lighting, parks maintenance, street trees, and more. Millosovich explained the priorities within the department had been handed down to him from Dave Frankel, who retired on October 1 last year after more than 30 years on the job. “Nick has worked with the city for 13 years, so he really knows his stuff,” said Frankel. “Nick has the best demeanor; he never gets rattled. It’s important [in that position] because there are a lot of demands. He knows what’s important and how to deal with the emergencies we have.” “Our guys have an incredible Former Piedmont City Administrator Paul Benoit, who had worked with Millosovich closely before Benoit retired one year ago, praised him for his knowledge of the city’s infrastructure. “Nick is a long-time Public Works employee,” said Benoit. “What always impressed me about Nick was his quiet and steady manner, as well as his confidence and competence. To do that job well you have to have a deep understanding of Piedmont’s assets and infrastructure and you need to have a strong commitment to public service. Nick has those qualities.” “The irrepressible Dave Frankel is hard to replace, but Nick is fully up to the task,” Benoit said. When Millosovich formally took over the position, the city had just declared a state of emergency and implemented shelterin-place regulations due to the coronavirus. . “With our veteran crew, it’s been pretty simple, because they know exactly what needs to be done,” said Millosovich, adding that three members of his street department have each worked for the city for 30 years or longer. Marilyn Weber, Chair of the Piedmont Turkey Trot, the city’s second largest event after the 4th of July Parade, worked alongside Millosovich before he took on the title of supervisor. “Nick is such a kind, thoughtful and generous person,” she said. “I have had the pleasure of working with him as both a community member and as a volunteer on several community events and every interaction with Nick exceeds all expectations. He is a consummate professional and is very adept at dealing with many different circumstances. “The City of Piedmont is fortunate to have Nick leading the team,” Weber stated. Staff photo Nick Millosovich, Piedmont’s new Public Works Superintendent. capacity to do a lot of things. It’s a great team,” Frankel added with a strong sense of pride. One of the primary responsibilities as Supervisor will be to check sewer lines regularly through the year using a closed circuit television (CCTV) van. Millosovich and his crewmembers check for broken pipes, conduct spot repairs, and check storm drain lines. As testament to the work they do, Piedmont is the only city in a group of eight Bay Area cities that was not fined by the EPA for sewage leaking into the San Francisco Bay. But there is still work to be done. Once finished, about 85 percent of the city’s pipe system will be brand new. The public works department has still identified “problematic spots” throughout the city. “The bad pipes we have are still bad pipes, and we have a list of problematic spots throughout the city. We visit them at least once a year, and the ones along our creek lines are checked at least twice a year,” said Millosovich. Henry Lambert never got a chance to show what he can do. A junior and the leader of the Piedmont High School golf team this spring, his season was cut short due to the coronavirus. He was able to complete only one round of golf But deprived of interscholastic sports, Lambert isn’t taking any days off. He is competing in two different golf competitions this summer – the Junior Tour of Northern California and the Junior Golf Association of Northern California He is currently competing in the Johnny Miller Junior Championship at Napa’s Silverado Resort and is set to compete again on July 6 at the GANC/NCGA NorCal Players Championship at the legendary Pebble Beach. “I am competing in a bunch of tournaments this summer. I’m currently in Napa at the same place the PGA hosts the Safeway Open,” confirmed Lambert. “I’m just staying sharp; working on my short-game and hitting the ball straighter and controlling the curve of my shots,” he added. Before the COVID shutdown, Lambert shot one-under in their tri-match with San Leandro, Alameda, and Bishop O’Dowd. It was Piedmont High’s only match last spring. He has appeared in four tourneys this month, including two rounds of 75 at PGA course Cherry Island on June 23-24, then turned around to play in the June 25-26 Mountain View Jr. Championship at the Shoreline Golf Links, with rounds of 74 and 75. “I feel like I’ve been playing some of my best golf within the last couple of weeks. I think my best rounds are ahead of me,” added Lambert. Lambert, a team captain as a junior, earned an All-League selection as a sophomore. Entering his senior year, Lambert feels he has more control of his swing. “When I was younger, my swing at times would come from behind my body, which would force my ball to sway from the right to a hard left. Over the years, I’ve worked at coming at the ball straighter; it’s creating a straighter shot, “said Lambert. Soon to be a senior, Lambert will head to each of the courses around the Bay Area with added knowledge after playing most of them several times. “With how I’m playing lately, it feels that my experience on each course will help a lot.” Lambert heads into his senior year alongside classmate Nate Wilson, another four-year starter on the golf team. articles.text: Bryce Chu was named the North Coast Section’s Most Valuable Player after posting an 0.93 ERA and 18 strikeouts in the postseason. Pitcher Jordan Remer set a Piedmont High single-season record for strikeouts in 2008 with 102. This week, we look back at the Piedmont’s only North Coast Section champion baseball team back in 2008. It was the spring of 2008 the Boston Celtics beat the Los Angeles Lakers in six games, and Barack Obama was gearing up for his presidential run in the Democratic Primaries. But it was the Piedmont baseball that came out of nowhere to win the school’s only North Coast Section championship – then and now. The team didn’t win the league championship and was seeded No. 7 in the NCS post-season playoffs. They pulled off upset victories one after the other, eventually beating No. 1 Northgate in a game played at the Oakland Coliseum. “The Highlanders dogpiled in the infield. They pointed to the fans and family in the stands. Jordan Remer sat down on the grass with his head in his hands, overwhelmed by what the Highlanders just accomplished,” wrote the Post sportswriter Benjamin Bombard after the game. . To win the game, Piedmont tallied on two runs in each of the fourth, fifth, and sixth innings. Northgate piled on five runs in the fifth to take a 5-4 advantage, but Jeremy George, the underweight football quarterback that led the football and soccer teams to successful seasons, smacked a clutch two-run double over the head of the center fielder to take the lead in the sixth inning and win the game. George, PHS Class of 2009, was a three-sport star in high school, and opted to not play sports at UC San Diego. He was elected to the PHS Sports’ Hall of Fame in February 2020. Under first-year manager John Nelson, the Highlanders went 20-7-1 and finished second to St. Mary’s in the Bay Shore AthPhoto by Ken deCrosta letic League. Given a #7 seed, they began a series of dramatic post-season upsets, first defeating No. 2 St. Mary’s in the quarterfinals, then completely dominating No. 3 Campolindo in the semis, 13-7. Nelson was the school’s first coach after Mike Humphries retired after coaching baseball for roughly 30 years. Nelson left PHS following the 2009 season and became St. Mary’s head coach from 2011 to 2013. He closed his career there with a 7-6 win over Eric Olson’s Highlanders, which marked Olson’s first year at the school. Between Nelson’s departure and Olson’s arrival, PHS went 10-14 and 6-16 under Josh Muldau, then went 18-10 under Brent Weisbrod until losing to Nelson’s Panthers in the NCS quarterfinals. Olson has been at the helm for Piedmont ever since, making two NCS Finals appearances – his second was a 5-4 loss to Redwood Christian in 2018. Pied mont’s 2008 team received five All-League selections in the BSAL, including pitcher Bryce Chu receiving firstteam honors and NCS Most Valuable Player honors. Chu posted a 0.93 ERA throughout the NCS playoffs and struck out 18 batters. He was the closing pitcher in PHS’ 6-5 win over Northgate. Chu smacked a home run to centerfield in the NCS Semis and went 6-3 as a starting pitcher with 65 strikeouts. Remer was another firstteam selection and still holds the school’s single-season strikeout record with 102. Alexander Menke was another first-team selection with a 3.49 average, 22 hits, 26 runs, and two home runs. Piedmont first-year baseball John Nelson took the Highlanders to the school’s only NCS Title in 2008. He coached only two years in Piedmont. Ryan Patte and Kyle Bonacum were honorable mentions. Patte, the first baseman played the season without any errors, and Bonacum. the right fielder, finished with 16 hits.

14 Wednesday, July 1, 2020 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 13th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. Tennis player Angela Huang, PHS Class of 2019, completed her abbreviated freshman season at Washington University in St. Louis. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out alone. In the past I would work out with my trainer in Berkeley. Our athletic trainer from school helps us from afar. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Something I am proud of is that I was able to play in the lineup in college as a freshman for both singles and doubles. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Balancing sports in college is definitely not an easy thing to do, but it provides you with a unique experience many others don’t get to have. ANGELA HUANG Tennis CAMILLE CREIGHTON Softball What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main fitness goal for this summer is to maintain the strength and endurance that I had in my freshman season. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development through the tracking of weights, sets, and endurance for cardio exercises. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out on my own, but our trainer has developed the workouts for us from home. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone has been my ability to replicate squat and bench press weights with household objects, i.e. backpacks filled with textbooks. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? My advice: Don’t let COVID- 19 discourage you from staying active! Workouts come in many shapes and forms, and in these difficult times, it’s important to remember that hiking our local trails is just as beneficial as lifting in a gym. Piedmont High Class of 2019 Washington U. of St. Louis Class of 2023 Angela Huang had her freshman year at Washington University in St. Louis cut short after appearing in seven matches, after competing at No. 2 and 3 singles, while also playing No. 1 doubles alongside captain Ally Persky. Huang graduated from Piedmont High in 2019 after finishing her career as only the school’s second player to win back to back North Coast Section championships. She won the singles title in both Div. 1 and Div. 2, duplicating the feat of Kaelli Thiel in 2014-2015. She helped PHS complete its 20th consecutive undefeated League Championship, it was the final year of the school’s state record winning streak. In the Division 1 individual tournament, Huang won all four of her matches in straight sets after entering the brackets as an unseeded entrant. She made quick work of Camilla TarpeySchwed of Tamalpais in the finals, 6-1, 6-2. What is your workout program this summer? Our athletic trainer has given us weekly workouts to complete at home. They are of similar structure to the ones we do at school, but we are allowed to update it to adjust from working out at home. These workouts include body weight exercises and also weight-training routines. What are your fitness goals for this summer? To just stay in my best shape so that I’m ready to compete again in the fall, hopefully. Between stay-at-home orders, internships, and classes, it’s become even more important to keep tennis a top priority. How are you measuring your development? Each week we meet with our trainer online and discuss our workouts. A lot of our workouts include increasing intensity and weight, so that is how we can measure our progress. Piedmont High Class of 2019 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2023 Camille Creighton finished her freshman softball season at Pomona-Pitzer after appearing in two of the 11 games before the COVID shutdown. She graduated from Piedmont High in 2019 after starting on varsity all four years and took over at shortstop as a senior. Creighton was a three-time firstteam All-League selection and also received a second-team selection as a senior. Creighton helped win back-toback undefeated league championships in 2017 and 2018, which got the program promoted to the WACC’s upper Foothill Division in 2019. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program this summer is run through the app Teambuildr. Our workouts rotate between body weight circuits and cardio exercises. CAL BARNA Baseball & Football Cal Barna prepares for his senior campaign at Piedmont High as a twosport athlete in baseball and football. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goals include gaining 10-15 pounds to increase my strength tremendously, and being able to settle myself and truly focus when pitching. How are you measuring your development? I have metrics in certain lifts or workouts. Progress from the start to the end of the summer is based on how these numbers improve. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? With friends for lifting, a coach for pitching, and teammates for football. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Pitching 91 mph consistently, benching 230 pounds for film purposes, and throwing a baseball 365 feet. Prior to the COVID shutdown I could complete 12 pull ups; now, I am currently at 40. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Work harder than what you initially think is necessary. Don’t worry about your peers or feel pressure from what they are doing. This week’s look at five museums around the globe explores some of the most visited museums in Africa, South America, and Asia. You can visit all of them virtually as we continue to shelter in place. also spurred a debate amongst the art world: many scholars called for museums throughout Europe to return thousands of artifacts looted from Africa during the colonial period. You can learn more about the museum’s history by watching CGTN Africa’s introductory video at https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=Eri0OMwG-es Museum of Black Civilizations, Dakar, Senegal The Museum of Black Civilizations, inaugurated in 2018, acts as a creative hub for Senegal as well as the entire African continent. The museum both celebrates African cultures while detailing the struggle their people have faced throughout history. articles.text: The Guardians is John Grisham’s 40th novel. In most, he focuses on some aspect of legal practice and he always educates the reader about both the necessary legal procedures and the many ways that practitioners elude or obscure the intent of the law. Here Grisham writes about a lawyer who seeks release for prisoners who have been wrongly convicted. The subject is close to Grisham’s heart because he has served on the Board of the Innocence Project, which seeks to reverse the convictions of innocent inmates. In the novel, the characters speculate that this happens in about 10% of cases, which means that there may be thousands of innocent people in prison today. Grisham is a master of characterization, plot, narrative and dialogue. Here he introduces Cullen Post, a sweet and caring man who is both a lawyer and, after a nervous breakdown, an Episcopal priest. Post is building a legal case to introduce new evidence that will lead to the release of a Black man named Quincy Miller who was framed for the murder of a Florida lawyer. The story wanders through a collection of interesting individuals – Southern lawyers who drink too much, weak prison guards who have been corrupted by dangerous criminals, forthright women in power, and angry officials who don’t want to admit they are wrong. All are well described but none are so overwhelmingly evil that they are unbelievable. This novel does not have the astonishing turns of plot found in Grisham’s early novels such as The Firm, but it is a well-constructed, engaging narrative with characters that one might like to know. It is also a painless and detailed way to learn about the way the legal system malfunctions for many people. Ann McCauley studied Anthropology at Cal and works in international health. She loves stories with sympathetic, wise characters who engage in humorous conversations and travel to exotic places.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Life is fragile, tenuous, each day a gamble. Until it isn’t. The idea that bad things happen to good people is an abstraction. Suddenly what we take for granted – another dawn, and all that follows – can no longer hold our weight, like fragile ice on a winter’s pond. Still Alice is about such a life; it may be more truth than some viewers care to confront in a film. The movie is a tour de force by Julianne Moore. She portrays Dr. Alice Howland, a professor of linguistics at Colombia University, married to John (Alec Baldwin), a research scientist. She is the mother of three lovely children (Kristen Stewart, Kate Bosworth and Hunter Parrish). Accomplished, cherished by her family and colleagues, just 50, she relishes in every way this moment in her life. But ever so gradually she begins to notice small moments when her memory hits a speed bump. What was automatic – a word during a lecture, the destination of a morning run – eludes her. And so begins a cruel and insidious journey, one in which all that she is, all that she has become, begins to abandon her. With John, she visits a neurologist who confirms that she has familial early onset Alzheimer’s disease. It’s a betrayal of her mind that is unexpected and will be, with unyielding certainty, catastrophic. Like a flower in full bloom, every pedal vibrant with life, she begins to close ever so slowly. What is so tragic is that Alice – bright, scholarly, educated, loving – is told in detail what awaits her. The path that stretches before her is detailed, like a photograph of familiar colors and images left out in the sunshine that slowly begins to fade. The irony of the film is its title: Still Alice. From the moment of her diagnosis, when she is told that the disease she has is very rare and also genetic (it’s possible that the gene she inherited came from her father, an alcoholic, and she may have passed it on to her children), Alice is no longer still Alice. She is now that person who struggles to find the courage and grace to face each day, to suffer each moment of forgetfulness, clinging to any remnant of who she was and wishes she still could be. Though this subject matter is not unique (recall The Notebook), what gives Still Alice its deeply human essence is the performance by Moore. She has been nominated for an Oscar as Best Actress. She is remarkable and restrained and finally a broken mirror. The camera lingers on her in tight, intimate shots, her every feature conveying the hope and sheer terror and brief moments of panic and lucidity that are now her life’s experiences. Moore is astonishing. She is just so good. As is the film, which is never gratuitous or purposively maudlin or sentimentalized. Do the filmmakers flinch? Of course. It’s just too hard. Yet when we leave the theater and look around and remember to breathe we know that we have been given one more day. A gift. As well as a thoughtful and moving story to ponder. Still Alice. It’s a betrayal of her mind that is unexpected and will be, with unyielding certainty, catastrophic. Like a flower in full bloom, every pedal vibrant with life, she begins to close ever so slowly. What is so tragic is that Alice – bright, scholarly, educated, loving – is told in detail what awaits her. The path that stretches before her is detailed, like a photograph of familiar colors and images left out in the sunshine that slowly begins to fade. The irony of the film is its title: Still Alice. From the moment of her diagnosis, when she is told that the disease she has is very rare and also genetic (it’s possible that the gene she inherited came from her father, an alcoholic, and she may have passed it on to her children), Alice is no longer still Alice. She is now that person who struggles to find the courage and grace to face each day, to suffer each moment of forgetfulness, clinging to any remnant of who she was and wishes she still could be. Though this subject matter is not unique (recall The Notebook), what gives Still Alice its deeply human essence is the performance by Moore. She has been nominated for an Oscar as Best Actress. She is remarkable and restrained and finally a broken mirror. The camera lingers on her in tight, intimate shots, her every feature conveying the hope and sheer terror and brief moments of panic and lucidity that are now her life’s experiences. Moore is astonishing. She is just so good. As is the film, which is never gratuitous or purposively maudlin or sentimentalized. Do the filmmakers flinch? Of course. It’s just too hard. Yet when we leave the theater and look around and remember to breathe we know that we have been given one more day. A gift. As well as a thoughtful and moving story to ponder. Still Alice. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Like its Pixar antecedents – Ratatouille, The Incredibles, Monsters, Finding Nemo, Cars and the incomparable Wall-E – Up will delight and entertain audiences of all ages. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail breathtaking, and the story a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, square-faced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed. Years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. All that is absent from this touching retrospective is that one, magnificent adventure. Sadly, having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties some 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning he floats away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, well-equipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of lift-off. And so the journey begins with the unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. You can’t make this stuff up. Well, actually, in the case of Pixar, you can, and that is exactly what these filmmakers do with unbridled imaginations and an inexhaustible well of stories that captivate and entertain. In Up they even manage to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell. Carl uses a poignant aphorism about how life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). Up. Animated, with voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. Written and Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Petersen. Pixar Studios, 2009. Rated PG. articles.text: Musicians have always led the best of lives. We have friends everywhere. We get to travel and eat good food. After all, as Shakespeare once said: “ If music be the food of love, play on.” In times like these, some inspiration is needed. Let’s sample the good life as exemplified by some famous musicians. Rossini must be mentioned first, because he was the most famous gourmet of all - and a notable gourmand as well. But first we need some music to whet our appetites. The German composer Handel was a noted gourmand. He wrote music for virtually every festive occasion – sailing, fireworks, eating and more. It didn’t matter what the occasion was, Handel wrote for it. On the other hand, history does not include Telemann as a gourmand, but he was more specific when it came to the music. After all, Telemann’s most famous composition is Tafel Musik (music for the banquet). Beginning with breakfast, we would expect some good espresso. Johann Sebastian Bach wrote a miniature opera which is known to us as the “Coffee Cantata”. This is a tongue-in-cheek satire in praise of coffee and the addiction thereof. So, get the espresso ready. Don’t let anyone tell you that Bach was devoid of humor. The hero of this satirical opera is a character named Stick In The Mud. To accompany this good espresso, may I suggest Melba toast. Opera singers have been the inspiration for many famous dishes, and Melba toast was named for the Australian opera singer Nellie Melba. She was always watching her weight, so the noted chef Escoffier invented a twicebaked toast especially for Melba. Strangely, the other dish named for Melba is the extremely rich Peach Melba. Escoffier’s original version is a large portion of vanilla ice cream topped with a lightly poached peach and that topped with sweetened raspberry sauce. Let me offer a less caloric version of Peach Melba. Mix equal amounts of ricotta cheese and cream cheese. Add sugar to taste. Put a half peach on top of your cheese mixture and top it off with some raspberry jam. This is the easy version of Peach Melba, and it is just about as good as the original version. Returning to the great Rossini as gourmet-gourmand, we must select tornadoes of beef a la Rossini. The recipe appeared in one of my previous columns, but it is easy to find on the Internet. When you prepare these tornadoes, be sure to use the very finest fillet of beef available. The original recipe calls for fois gras, but you could substitute pate fois gras if you like. Now, for the main course. Two more opera stars figure in our Gourmet Hall of Fame. Soprano Luisa Tetrazzini takes credit for the dish named for her, Chicken Tetrazzini. Her friend, the immortal Neapolitan tenor A gala dinner in the Parisian home of virtuoso violinist Pablo de Sarasate on Sept. 29, 1907. Sarasate’s house was designed by the artist Janes McNeil Whistler. The guests included the famed female violinist Teresina Tua and composer Enrique Fernandez-Arbos. Enrico Caruso, offers a contribution with Spaghetti a la Caruso. For this one all you need is spaghetti with marinara sauce. Mix in some lightly sautéed chicken livers and you have Chicken a la Caruso. If you don’t like chicken livers, leave them out and enjoy spaghetti marinara. Caruso loved his hometown of Naples, but he refused to sing there. At his operatic debut, the Neapolitans gave him a very cool reception. He said he would go to Naples only to eat spaghetti, but he would never sing for them. Two of the most successful virtuosos were the Spanish violinist Pablo de Sarasate and the Polish pianist Ignatz Jan Paderewski. Both were so successful that they traveled in their own private railroad cars. Paderewski’s was plushly appointed and included a drawing room to play cards and a fully stocked kitchen. Needless to say, butlers were engaged on every trip. A menu from one of Sarasate’s banquets accompanies this article. And now for dessert One of Sarasate’s Spanish dances is a song in praise of chocolate. The Spanish version is hot drinking chocolate thickened with cornstarch. If you wanted, you could encore peach melba or take inspiration from the French pianist-composer Saint-Saens. One of his most brilliant compositions is another satire in music. You can just about taste the whipped cream in this effervescent trifle. It is called “Wedding Cake,” a strange combination for a man who had no interest in women. So…Whether you are a gourmet or a gourmand or just a “grazer”, I leave you with the absolute final thought on the subject of food. The English would call something like this a savory. Noted social critic Weird Al Yankovic said it all in his seminal opus “Eat it” – just eat it. Enjoy. Next week: The contradictions of music and why you should play a musical instrument.

The short version of the story from here is that British merchants looked south to Portugal to fill the wine gap. It was the red varietals of the Douro, which had the additional benefit of river transport over mountainous land passage, that came to be preferred. For the wine to survive the sea voyage, however, it needed to be fortified – spiked with a brandy that increased the alcohol content and served as a preservative. What started as necessity was cultivated into style. Brandy came to be added earlier, in effect stopping the fermentation process so that more residual sugar remained and the end result is a wine at once sweet and high octane. There are many variations of port and tasting the range of styles is one of the treats of the Douro. Smaller producers such as Alves de Sousa, once a supplier of grapes to larger houses and now an independent estate, continue the port tradition with a strong sense of family heritage. The 20-year-old tawny port from Alves de Sousa is the handiwork of three generations of winemakers. For another taste of Portugal, I recommend the pastries. There is the pastéis de nata, a bite-sized wonder of layers of flaky crust with egg custard filling and the lightest of toasted, caramelized topping. Legend has it that they started at Mosterio dos Jerónimos in Lisbon and that the recipe was sold by a monk to a bakery in the city’s Belém district. Pastéis de nata are found across the country, alongside highly localized delights. Near Lisbon there are Sintra’s travesseiros, translated roughly as “pillows.” Dusted in a light sprinkling of sugar and cinnamon these almond cream fillings are couched in layers of dough. In Amarante, the crossing point between the Douro and Minho wine regions, confeitarias line the cobblestone streets of 31 de Janeiro like Starbucks in New York. It is impossible to leave one without walking into another. The train-station city of Pinhão remains at the center of Portugal’s Douro, and port, region. With layers of flakey crust and an egg custard filling, pastéis de nata (center) are Portugal’s flag-bearing pastry in a country filled with regional delights.

By Kate Fratar In the world market, the most easily recognizable Portuguese product may be port. The sweet, fortified wine comes from the Douro valley, traditionally traveling by rabelo, a long cargo boat, to Vila Nova de Gaia for storage before being shipped from Porto. The hitch in claiming port as thoroughly Portuguese is that the history of the wine is at least half British. Trade between the two nations goes back centuries, with the 1386 Treaty of Windsor as a cornerstone. Geopolitical motivations aside, the treaty also buttressed a growing commercial relationship by granting each country the right to trade on the same terms as subjects of that country and encouraging settlement with the right for subjects of either country to dwell in the domain in the other. The 20-year-old tawny port from Alves de Sousa is the handiwork of three generations of winemakers. For another taste of Portugal, I recommend the pastries. There is the pastéis de nata, a bite-sized wonder of layers of flaky crust with egg custard filling and the lightest of toasted, caramelized topping. Legend has it that they started at Mosterio dos Jerónimos in Lisbon and that the recipe was sold by a monk to a bakery in the city’s Belém district. Pastéis de nata are found across the country, alongside highly localized delights. Near Lisbon there are Sintra’s travesseiros, translated roughly as “pillows.” Dusted in a light sprinkling of sugar and cinnamon these almond cream fillings are couched in layers of dough. In Amarante, the crossing point between the Douro and Minho wine regions, confeitarias line the cobblestone streets of 31 de Janeiro like Starbucks in New York. It is impossible to leave one without walking into another. There, one of the concoctions to come out of mixing sugar and egg yolks is a cookie named ponte after the Roman bridge. For the best news of all, yes, many of these delicacies would go well with port. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Mexican rice from Diana Kennedy’s cookbook, My Mexican Kitchen. Diana Kennedy is one of my culinary heroes. There’s a recently released documentary film Diana Kennedy: Nothing Fancy that’s available to stream from home. The film is an insightful telling of the feisty Kennedy’s life and travels throughout Mexico. Kennedy, now 97 is British, but has spent most of her adult life living in Mexico; and is widely recognized as the world’s leading authority on Mexican cuisine. Her most approachable recipes are from My Mexican Kitchen, Techniques and Ingredients. It is from this book that I prepare her Arroz a la Mexicana; the familiar rice served at your favorite Mexican restaurant, and easy to prepare to enjoy at home. Whilst Diana will surely chide one for using canned, crushed tomatoes in place of fresh, I say go with what is most flavorful and available. Vine-ripened tomatoes that taste truly tomato-y are available in our summer months, but many are still cooking out of the “pandemic pantry”. I’ve halved the ingredients from the cookbook’s recipe as I most frequently cook for two these days. Just double the ingredients if you need to scale it up for a larger quantity. Arroz a la Mexicana Makes 3 cups Adapted from Diana Kennedy’s My Mexican Kitchen INGREDIENTS • 3/4 cup long-grain white rice • 2 tablespoons vegetable oil • 3/4 cup ripe tomatoes, coarsely chopped • 1 tablespoon white onion, coarsely chopped • 1 clove fresh garlic, coarsely chopped • 1-1/2 cup chicken broth • 1/4 – 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • 1 tablespoon peas (optional) • 1 serrano chile (optional) INSTRUCTIONS 1. Pour hot water to cover the rice and let soak for about 5 minutes. Strain, rinse in cold water and strain again, shaking the strainer to remove any excess water. Do this when ready to cook the rice, not ahead of time, to minimize the rice absorbing too much water. 2. Place the tomatoes, onion, and garlic in a blender jar and blend until smooth. Set aside. 3. Heat the oil in a heavy 2-quart saucepan over medium heat. The one I use is about 3-inches deep and 8-1/2 inches in diameter. Stir in the rice – it should sizzle as it hits the oil.

Amazing progress has been made in the past 20 years, and the vast majority of these wines are now much better than they were years ago. It took a while to find the right growing areas and to develop the right vineyard management techniques, but many of these wines rival their French cousins. This year, the top wines from the tasting list include a couple of perennial favorites plus some really interesting newcomers. articles.text: Spike in reported COVID cases; total in county nears 6,000 Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials on Monday, June 29, as concerns mount about COVID-19 hospitalizations. The new order does not reverse previous reopening orders, but the county is now postponing its plan to phase in the next stage of reopening. The number of COVID-19 cases in Alameda County was 5,964 as of yesterday, Tuesday, June 30, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. There have been 824 new cases since last week, a 16 percent increase. Another 15 people have died of the disease since last Tuesday, June 23, increasing the number of total fatalities to 135. Alameda County continues to be hardest hit county in the San Francisco Bay Area. Santa Clara County, the initial epicenter in the region, now counts 4,370 cases and 156 total deaths. In San Francisco, the caseload is 3,603 and there have been 50 deaths. No new cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, were reported in Piedmont in June. In total, there have been 13 cases reported in Piedmont. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, 2,352 cases were reported. Hayward now has a total of 987. Fremont has reported 290 cases and San Leandro has also reported 290. In its announcement about pausing the county’s reopening schedule this week, the Alameda County Public Health Department noted that the case rate per 100,000 people had increased from 63.2 to 71.1. Daily hospitalizations had been decreasing through Monday, June 22, but have been increasing daily since then. “We recognize the multifaceted challenges presented by a slow reopening and are grateful for the sustained effort and sacrifices made by our residents and businesses,” the department said in a statement. “As the pandemic evolves, we will need to remain flexible and nimble in our response.” While the county had been opening up new sectors of the economy about every two weeks, that plan has been put on hold for the time being. The department said that this week and next week will be critical for assessing how and when to reopen more activities. An order that went into place on June 19 allowed for outdoor museums, outdoor restaurant dining, some religious services, indoor retail, mall shopping and outdoor fitness classes. The timetable for reopening activities such as indoor dining, barber shops, pools and gyms is now delayed until further notice. The surge of COVID-19 cases across the state over the past few weeks has caused officials on all levels in California to act to reduce the spread of the disease, a shift from earlier hopes that the pandemic was trending toward its endpoint. “Until recently, our state managed to do so well that our experience has been dubbed ‘The California Miracle,’” tweeted University of California, San Francisco Department of Medicine Chair Bob Wachter on Monday, June 29. “But let’s say it clearly: The Miracle is over. The sooner we acknowledge that, the better off we’ll be.” While Wachter said state officials and residents mostly acted responsibly, relaxing restrictions starting in mid-May appears to have led to increases in cases. The new order does not reverse previous reopening orders, but the county is now postponing its plan to phase in the next stage of reopening. In San Francisco, the caseload is 3,603 and there have been 50 deaths. No new cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, were reported in Piedmont in June. In total, there have been 13 cases reported in Piedmont. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, 2,352 cases were reported. Hayward now has a total of 987. Fremont has reported 290 cases and San Leandro has also reported 290. In its announcement about pausing the county’s reopening schedule this week, the Alameda County Public Health Department noted that the case rate per 100,000 people had increased from 63.2 to 71.1. Daily hospitalizations had been decreasing through Monday, June 22, but have been increasing daily since then. “We recognize the multifaceted challenges presented by a slow reopening and are grateful for the sustained effort and sacrifices made by our residents and businesses,” the department said in a statement. “As the pandemic evolves, we will need to remain flexible and nimble in our response.” While the county had been opening up new sectors of the economy about every two weeks, that plan has been put on hold for the time being. Anything less will result in a tantrum of epic proportions.” The prophets inveighed against the construction and worship of idols. These distracted from the worship of the One God who alone was worthy of respect. These were invitations to forget the One God’s resolute commitment to justice, care for the downtrodden and concern for the well-being of widows and orphans. The Roman Emperor’s visage on a coin was problematic to Jesus and his contemporaries. Jesus acknowledged that there wasn’t much he could do to undo this act of arrogant grandiosity, but he refused to be subservient to the Emperor. His words were, “Give to Caesar that which is Caesar’s, but reserve for God that which is God’s.” In a profoundly inhumane manner, the Roman Empire erected the crucified as temporary statues. Statues to the power of the state. Statues warning against insurrection. Statues declaring who it was that deserved to be treated as human and who did not. Statues that stood sentinel against dreams of a better day for the people of the land. The word statue comes to us from Latin via Old French. It has to do with that which is represented in metal, and that which is set up. This etymology reminds us that statues have a history. They do not spontaneously evolve in a particular time, in a particular place, in a particular way. They are made. They are set up. They are created to send a message. The message statues send is often problematic. The Bible understands this. Hence, its caution in their regard. The Bible understands that human beings are very complex, that our motives are often less than pure. Thus, it urges us to be very careful about how we enshrine ourselves, how we tell our story. Rev. articles.text: On Wednesday June 24 at 2 p.m. a man in his late twenties walked into Mulberry’s Market without wearing a mask. He began talking nonsensically to a manager and then became unruly and angry at the counter. Mulberry’s General Manager Sal Viveros stepped in and told him multiple times that he needed to leave if he refused to comply with the State of California order to wear a mask. The man jumped towards Viveros and punched him. Two staff members behind the counter quickly pulled the man off of the manager and got him down to the ground. On his way down to the floor, the suspect grabbed a bottle off a display and tried to smash it on the employees. He ended up breaking the bottle and cutting his own hand. The cut spilled quite a bit of blood onto the floor. Two staff members held him down until the police got there about 90 seconds later. The police determined that he required medical attention and was taken to the hospital. He was cited for vandalism, assault and a health violation. Mulberry’s intends to press charges.
